forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Lambeth forecasts £9.303m overspend at June, £1.676m better than month two, with parking £6.2m short
news_drafts.lead:
Lambeth Council is forecasting that it will spend £9.303m more than its general budget allows in 2026-27, according to the first-quarter financial report going to Cabinet on 23 September. The figure, as at the end of June, is £1.676m better than the forecast at the end of month two, which the report calls a "favourable movement".

The report says the council's largest single shortfall is in income. Growth and Environment is forecasting an £8.603m overspend, £0.720m worse than at month two. The report says the pressure is "mainly driven by a shortfall against income targets", which total £10.077m across the directorate. Parking is the biggest part: a £6.712m income target against a forecast of £0.5m, which the report attributes to "paused schemes, increased compliance and a reduction in PaybyPhone transactions". Parks events (£1.2m, from cancelled events), markets (£0.6m), CCTV (£0.4m) and sports facilities (£0.4m) also fall short. Management action to find £9.9m of mitigation is still being developed.

Elsewhere, Children, Families and Education pressure is "largely from placements and SEN transport", and the temporary accommodation overspend comes from delays in starting new savings work, which the report expects to be achieved fully in 2027-28. In Resources, Finance has been slow to deliver staffing savings.

The council has a £116m package of exceptional financial support (government permission to borrow to cover day-to-day spending), approved in February 2026, plus £40m for its housing account. Because of this, it expects quarterly meetings with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, and an independent review by the accountancy body CIPFA is under way. Cabinet is also asked to note the use of up to £3.903m of flexible capital receipts (one-off money from asset sales) to support budget proposals, and a review of the capital programme to minimise future borrowing.

The dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) is forecast to end March 2027 with a net deficit of £11.225m, driven by high needs spending (support for children with special educational needs and disabilities).

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forecast £2.5m surplus from reduced borrowing costs and void losses; HRA more stable than General Fund
findings.detail: The HRA is forecast to achieve a £2.544m surplus in 2026-27, driven by lower PWLB interest rates on refinanced debt and reduced void losses. This represents the HRA is operationally performing better than the General Fund and managing its tenant base effectively.
findings.matters: Provides offsetting positive news; shows HRA management is functioning; however, improvement is due to external interest rate environment rather than operational change, so may not persist.
findings.figures: £2.544m HRA surplus forecast; includes £18m of £27m disrepair provision
findings.quote: The HRA is currently forecast to achieve £2.544m surplus for 2026/27. The forecast includes £18m of the £27m provision to account for the ongoing financial pressures associated with resolving the historic housing disrepair claims.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection 0.8% below profile at Q1 with £1.8m billing delays; resident affordability pressures evident
findings.detail: Council Tax collection at end Q1 was £581k below profile. The council notes 'broader economic and affordability pressures affecting taxpayers' ability to maintain payments' with increased direct debit failures and cancelled payment arrangements. Valuation Office delays in banding 875 new properties has also caused an estimated £1.8m in billing delays.
findings.matters: Council Tax is the council's most reliable and stable funding source. Collection below profile combined with stated affordability pressures suggests this will persist; £1.8m billing delay means income recognition is also delayed.
findings.figures: £581k shortfall at Q1; £1.8m estimated unbilled from property banding delays
findings.quote: This all tends to indicate a broader economic and affordability pressures affecting taxpayers' ability to maintain payments. In addition, the Valuation Office delays in banding new Council Tax properties (875) is delaying billing, this is estimated at £1.8m unbilled based on band D.

findings.headline: General Fund earmarked reserves remain low despite EFS top-up; stated to offer little financial resilience
findings.detail: Although the General Fund Balance is now at the S151 officer's recommended minimum (10% of net revenue expenditure) following EFS, earmarked revenue reserve levels are explicitly described as 'low and offer little financial resilience in the context of the challenges ahead.' This leaves the council with minimal buffer for unexpected costs or demand spikes.
findings.matters: Low reserves mean the council cannot absorb unexpected pressures or revenue shortfalls. The council is one significant adverse event away from requiring further government support.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance at ~10% of expenditure (minimum recommended); earmarked reserves characterised as 'low'
findings.quote: Although, following the approval of EFS, General Fund Balance is now around the level recommended by the S151 officer (10% of net revenue expenditure), earmarked revenue reserve levels remain low and offer little financial resilience in the context of the challenges ahead.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation savings of £5.5m not being achieved in 2026-27; implementation delays pushing full impact to 2027-28
findings.detail: Housing Services (General Fund) is forecasting a £5.6m overspend, driven by Temporary Accommodation. Planned savings through long leases (£1.5m), nightly paid reductions (£4.8m before offsets), and incentive schemes (£3m) are not being implemented on schedule. The council now expects full year savings only in 2027-28.
findings.matters: Temporary Accommodation is the council's highest-cost service and primary savings target. Implementation delays indicate the transformation programme cannot execute its core financial plans on time.
findings.figures: £5.576m Housing Services overspend; £1.5m long lease, £1.5m transfer, £1m housing company savings all delayed
findings.quote: Due to the delay to date in their implementation, the total 2026/27 saving is unlikely to be fully achieved, however it is expected that the full year impact will be delivered in 2027-28.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit reaching £11.2m by March 2027; High Needs Block overspend driven by EHCP commitments
findings.detail: The DSG is forecast to end 2026-27 with a £11.225m cumulative deficit due to High Needs Block overspends. Increases in EHCP commitments and associated top-up costs continue to exceed funding. The council remains reliant on DSG statutory override arrangements, which hold deficits separately but are not a sustainable solution.
findings.matters: SEND pressures are not being managed within budget, indicating demand-led costs are growing faster than funding. This is a recurring structural deficit in an area of rising national demand.
findings.figures: £11.225m net DSG deficit forecast at 31 March 2027; £13.4m in-year overspend
findings.quote: This would leave a net DSG deficit position at 31st March 2027 of £11.225m.
